title: Po: memory trims its own readers via dummy cells
idea: Po: memory that calibrates the circuits that read it. At power-up each SA's offset is measured by repeatedly sensing balanced bitlines, and a correction charge is written into a dedicated dummy cell on that bitline pair; before every sense the dummy wordline fires and pre-biases the bitline by exactly that offset, refreshed alongside normal refresh.
why: Periphery (#7) and capacitor wall (#1): cancels ~80% of SA Vt mismatch, so SA devices can be ~3x smaller or Cs ~30% lower; trim storage costs one row per subarray instead of fuses or analog trim DACs.

title: Gigahertz CCD loops: one floating-diffusion amp per 64 bits
idea: Failure mined: 1970s CCD memories (Fairchild, Intel 2416) lost to DRAM on millisecond serial latency and charge-transfer loss. Fix: 64-stage buried-channel CCD loops with imaging-grade transfer efficiency (>99.9999%), 2-phase clocked at 4 GHz (worst-case 16 ns rotation), each sensed and re-injected by one floating-diffusion amplifier. Packets hold 2 bits (4 charge levels), and there are no per-bit contacts, capacitors or wordline drivers.
why: 10x at the same cost: ~2F^2 per packet vs 6F^2 (3x) x 2 bits per packet (2x) x periphery shrinking from 49% to ~10% (~1.7x) = ~10x. Built with CMOS-image-sensor masks (no capacitor module, little EUV) in U.S. image-sensor fabs.

title: Normally-on wordline clamps turn IGZO DRAM non-volatile for months
idea: Constraint: non-volatile, using a capacitor cell. Oxide-semiconductor (IGZO) access transistors leak ~1e-20 A, so the only threat when power drops is wordlines floating up. Each wordline gets a depletion-mode IGZO pull-down held off by the live supply; when power vanishes it turns on by itself and clamps every wordline to ground, giving months of unpowered retention.
why: NV with DRAM endurance and speed, no ferroelectric wear, and a periphery cost of one tiny device per wordline driver; refresh shrinks to a power-up scrub (fact 3).

title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout replaces bitline charge sharing
idea: First principles: a 5 fF cell at 0.5 V holds ~15,600 e-, yet CMOS image sensors resolve ~1 e- because they fully TRANSFER charge onto a ~0.5 fF floating diffusion instead of sharing it with a ~40 fF bitline. Build the DRAM cell as a pinned storage node + transfer gate into a floating diffusion shared by 4-8 cells, read by a local source follower (~300 uV/e-), so a ~500 e- (0.1 fF) cell gives a ~150 mV signal.
why: Breaks the capacitor charge wall (fact 1): required Cs drops ~30x, so pillars no longer need AR 60-75:1 and 3D tiers get far easier; periphery SA offset budget relaxes.

title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout replaces charge sharing with full transfer
idea: Effect: complete charge transfer onto a tiny node (the CMOS image-sensor 4T pixel principle). Every 16 cells share a ~0.3 fF floating diffusion behind a transfer gate and a one-transistor source follower; the cell charge is dumped fully onto the tiny node instead of being shared with a ~50 fF bitline. The follower drives the bitline as a voltage, and correlated double sampling removes kTC reset noise.
why: Capacitor wall (fact 1): signal per electron rises ~30x, so Cs could drop to ~1 fF (AR ~15:1), removing high-AR capacitor steps.

title: Image-sensor ramp comparators replace per-bitline DRAM latch sense amps
idea: Substitute per-bitline cross-coupled latches with the column-parallel single-slope ramp comparator borrowed from CMOS image sensors. The bitlines act as analog sample-and-hold nodes, one comparator plus counter serially digitizes 16 bitlines against a global ramp, and a burst write driver then restores the row.
why: Periphery area: SA count drops 16x, cutting sense strip area by about 60%; slower random access suits streaming AI weight memory where bandwidth matters more than latency.

title: CCD charge shifting replaces bitlines for column readout
idea: Substitute the bitline with a polysilicon charge-coupled column: stored charge packets are clocked down the column like a CCD imager to a single floating-diffusion sense node at the column end. This revives 1970s CCD memory for sequential AI streams with two-level poly in a university fab.
why: Periphery and charge wall: one SA per column instead of per bitline pair, and floating-diffusion gain lets small packets be sensed.

title: Cooperative-harvester wordlines: one charge-and-float driver serves four mats
idea: Farmers share one combine across fields. A sub-wordline driver charges a wordline to 3 V through a bootstrapped pass gate and then disconnects; the wordline floats high on its own capacitance for the ~30 ns row-open time while the same driver serves wordlines in three other mats.
why: Sub-wordline driver strips are ~10-15% of die; sharing one across four mats cuts them ~3x, a ~7-10% die shrink (fact 7).

title: Line-shaft wordline boost: one resonant tank powers every subarray
idea: Like a mill's line shaft driving every machine through belts, replace dozens of local VPP charge pumps with one package-level LC resonator (off-chip inductor plus on-chip capacitance). Its ~3 V sinusoid is tapped by bootstrap rectifiers at each sub-wordline driver strip, all built in 180 nm.
why: Local pumps waste ~60-70% of their energy and take ~3-5% of die; resonant delivery recycles wordline charge, cutting VPP energy ~2x and pump area ~70%.

title: Standardize a raw-tolerant DRAM grade with soft-bit interface
idea: Box: any cell x any access x soft-output SA x host-side decoding x any substrate x any fab. Push a JEDEC-style spec, backed by CHIPS-funded qualification, for 'RT-DRAM' rated at 1% raw BER that exposes soft bits and moves ECC into the host or CXL controller, so suppliers can sell relaxed dies interchangeably.
why: Policy unlocks the relaxed-cell gains industry-wide and lets new U.S. entrants compete on cheaper relaxed processes.

title: Bitline segments become the successive-approximation capacitor DAC
idea: For multi-level read, split each bitline into binary-weighted segments (1:2:4 units of cells) with segment switches and perform charge-redistribution SAR using the bitline's own parasitic capacitance as the DAC; the parasitic that normally kills signal becomes the converter's reference.
why: Enables MLC DRAM sensing with ~zero added capacitor area; ~1.5-2x density at modest periphery cost (facts 1, 7).

title: Sculptor carving: subtractive dry-etched ruthenium/molybdenum periphery wiring
idea: Damascene copper is casting: pour into a mold, then grind and wash (CMP). Carve instead, like a sculptor: blanket-deposit Ru or Mo, pattern, and plasma-etch the periphery's local/intermediate wiring and contacts, then gap-fill with flowable low-k. No barrier, plating, CMP or post-CMP scrub.
why: Water: CMP plus post-CMP cleans, among the biggest UPW users per layer, fall ~10x on periphery metal levels; Mo contacts (U.S.-mined) also replace tungsten, easing the China-80% chokepoint.

title: Smart-pixel free-space optical page readout to processor
idea: Revive 1990s smart-pixel optical interconnect. Each sense-amp group drives a micro-LED or electro-absorption modulator on the memory die's backside, and a microlens array images the whole open page onto a photodetector array on the stacked processor, moving thousands of bits in parallel with no TSVs or serializers.
why: Removes the HBM TSV tax (fact 6) and serializer periphery, targeting <0.5 pJ/bit versus 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM (fact 5).

title: Roll-to-roll polymer waveguide flex carries memory traffic optically
idea: Worse: push every bit through lossy copper with power-hungry SerDes equalizers. Flip: laminate a roll-to-roll-embossed polymer waveguide flex between memory stacks and the processor package, coupled to micro-LED or VCSEL transmitters on the memory base die.
why: Data-movement energy (fact 5): sub-pJ/bit links over centimeters, letting memory sit farther from the accelerator and escape interposer area limits.

title: Compressed-sensing reads of sparse tensors with fewer sense ADCs
idea: Borrow compressive sampling from MRI and radio astronomy and shrink it to the column: in non-destructive gain-cell mats holding ReLU-sparse activations, the read currents of 8 columns are summed onto one sense line through pseudo-random +/-1 select patterns, taking 3 measurements per 8 columns, and a small base-die solver reconstructs the (at most 1-of-8 nonzero) data. Dense data falls back to normal column reads.
why: Cuts sense circuitry ~2.7x and read energy per useful bit for sparse AI data (facts 7, 8); applies to the 50-90% sparse share of activation traffic.

title: Pulse-echo bitline reads a whole column of gain cells at once
idea: Ideal result: one probe reads every cell on a line simultaneously. Treat a long bitline as a transmission line where each non-destructive gain cell loads it with a state-dependent impedance step; a 10 ps edge launched from the end returns a time-encoded echo train decoded by one comparator plus time-to-digital converter.
why: Periphery area (fact 7) and overfetch (fact 8): one sensing front end per 256+ cells instead of one SA per bitline pair, suited to column-streaming AI reads.

title: Sense amp fused with time-to-digital converter as retention canary
idea: Combine every sense-amp stripe with a shared 6-bit time-to-digital converter that timestamps how long each bitline pair takes to cross the latch threshold during ordinary activations; slow-resolving (low-charge) rows are logged in a small per-bank table and refreshed at 64 ms while all others drop to 256-1024 ms. Normal reads become free, continuous retention measurements, which also catches variable-retention cells that offline profiling misses.
why: Refresh (fact 3: 16-33% idle power, 10-20% bandwidth); in-field margin tracking could cut refresh operations ~4x.

title: Solar MPPT perturb-and-observe tracking of sense references
idea: Like a solar inverter hunting the maximum power point, each mat controller nudges its sense reference/precharge level by +/-5 mV on ECC-protected reads and keeps whichever direction lowers the corrected-bit count, so the reference follows temperature, aging and 1-vs-0 retention asymmetry.
why: Refresh: a centred reference reads decaying '1' cells correctly for longer, roughly doubling the refresh interval (refresh energy -50%, bandwidth +5-10%).

title: Laser-release bond layers let one bad tier be swapped
idea: Ideal result: a 3D memory whose layers come apart like building blocks. Insert a thin UV-absorbing release layer in each cell-on-periphery tier bond, so laser lift-off separates a failing tier and a known-good tier is re-bonded onto the same periphery.
why: 3D DRAM yield compounds per tier (fact 2): rework makes 26+ tiers economically tolerable and keeps the periphery tier in service.

title: Rosen piezoelectric transformer generates wordline voltage acoustically
idea: Revive the 1950s Rosen piezoelectric transformer as an AlN MEMS resonator in the package or interposer (AlN is CMOS-compatible and made in the U.S.). Driven at resonance from 1.1 V, it steps the voltage up acoustically to 3-4 V and replaces on-die Dickson charge pumps for the VPP and negative-wordline rails.
why: Frees the ~5-8% of die area spent on charge pumps and their decoupling (fact 7) and lifts VPP conversion efficiency from ~30% to ~70% (fact 10 energy).

title: Po: the charge pump lives in the package
idea: Po: a DRAM die with no charge pumps. Generate VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias in a package-level GaN or deep-trench-capacitor integrated-passive converter at ~85% efficiency and deliver them through dedicated bumps or hybrid-bond pads, deleting on-die pumps and their decoupling capacitors.
why: Periphery (#7) and voltage floor (#10): on-die pumps and decaps take ~5-8% of die and run ~30-40% efficient; moving them out frees area and roughly halves VPP energy.

title: Per-segment adaptive negative wordline bias tames the leakage tail
idea: Worse: hold every unselected wordline at the same off level so the leakiest 0.01% of cells set refresh for all. Flip: give each wordline segment a test-programmed negative off level (-0.2 to -0.4 V) from a small local bias generator, applying deep negative bias only where the tail lives.
why: Leakage tail forcing refresh (fact 3): ~10x tail suppression in hot spots stretches refresh 2-4x while sparing gate stress elsewhere.

title: Package-level GaN switched-capacitor rails replace on-die pumps
idea: Scale shift from die to package: VPP (~3 V) and the negative wordline bias come from a GaN switched-capacitor converter embedded in the package substrate through a dense bond/TSV grid, deleting the dozens of on-die charge pumps.
why: On-die pumps take several % of area at ~30-40% efficiency; ~90%-efficient package converters roughly halve wordline supply energy (fact 10) and free ~3-5% of die (fact 7).

title: K: potassium-ion oxide electret supplies permanent negative wordline bias
idea: Drift K+ ions into a SiO2 plate under each mat's negative-wordline rail or back gate and lock them with a nitride cap, forming a stable electret (as in MEMS harvesters) that supplies a built-in -0.3 to -0.5 V bias with no VBB/VNWL charge pump.
why: Removes a pump and its standby current and area; a negative wordline low suppresses the leakage tail (fact 3), lengthening refresh intervals.

title: Weak rows convert to twin-cell mode on the fly
idea: Ideal result: aging cells heal by teaming up. The row decoder can tie two physical rows into one logical row storing true and complement, so the SA sees a 2x differential signal; rows failing retention are downgraded to twin mode instead of being fused out.
why: Refresh tail (fact 3) and repair: rescues weak rows at a local 50% capacity cost and lets the whole die run a longer refresh period.

title: Analog activation integrators in wordline drivers stop row hammer
idea: Ideal result: a row that knows when its neighbors are in danger. Each sub-wordline driver adds a fixed charge quantum to a tiny leaky capacitor per activation; crossing a comparator threshold flags a targeted neighbor refresh, and the leak resets it at the refresh-window rate.
why: Row hammer (fact 9): exact per-row tracking at ~2% driver area instead of counter SRAM or 10-15% bandwidth for probabilistic schemes.

title: Image-sensor floating-diffusion readout with correlated double sampling
idea: Adopt CMOS image-sensor pixel readout: a transfer gate moves cell charge onto a ~0.5 fF floating diffusion read by a source follower, sampled before and after transfer (correlated double sampling) to cancel kTC noise and offset at ~2 electrons rms. A cell then needs only ~1,000 electrons (~0.15 fF at 1 V).
why: Capacitor charge wall (fact 1): Cs ~30x smaller, removing high-AR capacitor etch; the cost is a slower ~30-50 ns read, acceptable for a capacity tier.

title: Image-sensor column ADCs with CDS read two bits per cell
idea: Copy 50-megapixel phone sensors that digitize 1-electron-noise columns in parallel: every bitline pair gets a single-slope ADC sharing one global ramp, with correlated double sampling (sample at precharge, again after charge share) to cancel kTC noise and SA offset. Cells store four charge levels for 2 bits/cell.
why: Cost per bit and density up ~1.7-2x without a lithography shrink; refresh must run ~2x more often, partly offset by the CDS margin gain.

title: US DRAM entrant leads with 125 C automotive and defense grade
idea: A new US memory maker first targets Grade-1 (125 C) automotive, industrial and defense DRAM, where self-calibrating periphery is a moat, volumes suit a modest fab and prices are high, then scales to datacenter.
why: US manufacturability and capital intensity: profitable at lower volume, builds the learning curve before competing on commodity cost.

title: Plate-pulse charge boost during restore adds hot retention
idea: During restore, pulse the accessed mat's cell plate down by DeltaV, then release after the wordline closes: the storage node, now isolated, rises by ~DeltaV x Cs/(Cs+Cj), storing ~25% more charge without raising bitline voltage.
why: ~25% more charge = longer retention at 125 C or smaller Cs at equal retention (facts 1, 3).

title: EV battery-balancing capacitor ladder for stepwise bitline restore
idea: Borrowed from switched-capacitor active balancing in EV battery packs: bitlines are restored in three steps from a ladder of tank capacitors held at intermediate voltages, and on precharge they return charge down the same ladder instead of drawing everything from VDD.
why: Energy per bit (facts 8, 10): stepwise adiabatic charging cuts bitline restore energy ~2-3x, which matters most with 128x page overfetch.

title: Electrometer umbrella: bootstrapped guard lines erase bitline capacitance
idea: Electrometers hide cable capacitance under a guard 'umbrella' driven by a unity-gain copy of the signal. Route a guard trace in the metal level directly above each bitline (stacked, so no pitch cost) and drive it during charge sharing from a per-pair source follower that tracks the bitline, so the bitline-to-overlayer and contact coupling sees almost no voltage change.
why: Transfer ratio Cs/(Cs+C_BL): removing ~30-40% of effective bitline capacitance raises read signal ~1.5x, worth ~1.5 fF of Cs (lower capacitor AR) or ~50% longer bitlines with fewer SA strips.

title: Harmonic-telegraph frequency-division global data lines
idea: Revive Bell's and Gray's harmonic telegraph. Each subarray's secondary sense output modulates its own on-chip tone (1-8 GHz, from an injection-locked ring oscillator) onto one shared global data line, and the I/O block separates the channels with passive N-path filters. Eight banks' data share one wire instead of eight.
why: Cuts global data-bus wires and repeaters ~4-8x (fact 7 periphery area) and lets more banks run in parallel without adding wire area (fact 5).

title: Hadamard-coded multiplexed reads solve vertical ReRAM's sneak network
idea: Failure mined: vertical ReRAM (VRRAM) from Samsung and SanDisk stalled because sneak paths and IR drop worsened with every added plane. Fix: read all 64 cells of a pillar together with 64 measurements under Hadamard-coded +/- bias patterns on the word planes, then invert the known resistor-network model in a small periphery ASIC to recover each conductance. As in Hadamard spectroscopy, this gains ~sqrt(64) in SNR over one-at-a-time reads.
why: 10x at the same cost: 64 deposited planes per pillar etch become usable (VRRAM's whole premise) with ~8x SNR to spare, ~15x bits/mm^2 vs DRAM at 3D-NAND-like cost per mm^2. Latency is amortized because a pillar's 64 cells are read together.

title: DIMM PMIC delivers VPP and VBB, deleting on-die charge pumps
idea: Automotive and industrial boards push high-voltage generation into 180 nm BCD PMICs; DDR5 already moved 12 V to 1.1 V conversion onto the DIMM, so extend it by supplying ~3 V VPP and negative VBB on dedicated balls and deleting on-die pumps (30-40% efficient), keeping only local switches.
why: Die area -5-8% (fact 7) and pump energy ~2x better; the PMICs come from U.S. legacy BCD lines with no EUV.

title: CCFL piezoelectric transformer replaces wordline charge pumps
idea: Borrowed from the piezo transformers that drove LCD backlight lamps: an AlN bulk-acoustic resonator (the material of phone RF filters) steps a 1.1 V drive up to 3+ V at resonance, which is rectified into the wordline VPP rail.
why: Periphery and energy (facts 7, 10): charge pumps run ~30-40% efficient on ~2-4% of the die; piezo step-up targets ~70% efficiency in less area.

title: Room-temperature single-electron transistor electrometer per bitline segment
idea: Box: 0.5 fF planar MIM cap x IGZO access x SET electrometer x local segment sensing x SOI x e-beam/DSA-defined dots. A silicon-nanowire quantum-dot SET (dot <5 nm, charging energy >> kT) at each 32-cell bitline segment turns a few hundred electrons of signal into a large current swing, so the cell no longer needs a 60:1 pillar capacitor.
why: Capacitor charge wall: Cs can drop ~10x (5 fF to 0.5 fF), deleting the high-AR etch; local gain also shortens bitlines.

title: Ink-jet drop-on-demand cells: double-gated access opens one cell only
idea: Like a drop-on-demand print head that fires only the nozzles needed, give each access transistor two gates: a row gate (wordline) and an orthogonal column gate (column-select line). A cell conducts only at the row-AND-column intersection, so a 64-bit burst opens 64 cells and fires 64 SAs instead of 8,192.
why: Removes the 128x overfetch and the restore of untouched cells: ~50-100x less activate energy per useful bit, and row hammer weakens because full rows are never activated.

title: US periphery foundry-as-a-service for capacitorless memory startups
idea: Inverting 'each memory maker owns its fab end to end': a CHIPS-funded shared 28nm line runs standard sense/decode wafers and bonding for any capacitorless cell startup, paid per wafer, with guaranteed government purchase of first products.
why: Cuts a startup's capital need from $15B+ to array-only lines, builds US manufacturability and diversifies away from three incumbent DRAM makers.

title: Normally-off banks: domain-wall latches keep decoder and row state
idea: Constraint: nothing may be lost at power-off, periphery included. Mode registers, open-row addresses and decoder latches use magnetic domain-wall or FeFET latches, so a bank with an NV array power-gates completely between bursts and wakes in ~ns with no re-init or retraining.
why: Idle power: refresh (16-33% of idle) and periphery leakage go to ~0, a big gain for bursty AI-inference memory.

title: Dolphin unihemispheric sleep: mirrored hot pages across alternately refreshing subchannels
idea: Dolphins sleep one brain hemisphere at a time. The controller mirrors only the hottest ~1-2% of pages across the two DDR5 subchannels, refreshes them in alternation and steers reads to the awake copy, so refresh never stalls hot reads. Controller RTL plus FPGA evaluation, ~$400k in 18 months.
why: Fact 3: hides the refresh stalls behind the 10-20% bandwidth loss for latency-critical hot data, at a ~1-2% capacity cost.

title: Ground-precharge charge-transfer preamp triples bitline length
idea: Limit: no VDD/2 precharge or equalizer devices. Bitlines precharge to ground, and a charge-transfer transistor biased at its threshold pumps the cell's charge from the big bitline into a ~1 fF sense node, giving a voltage gain of about C_BL/C_SN (~10x) before a small latch.
why: Periphery: 3x longer bitlines (1,536 cells per BL) mean 3x fewer SA stripes (die -8-10%). An old trick revived for the long vertical bitlines of 3D DRAM (fact 2).

title: Error-correcting address codes keep decoders working after faults
idea: Ideal result: a decoder that cannot misfire. Encode each row address into a distance-3 code across the predecode lines, so a stuck predecode wire or broken gate still selects the correct row (or none, never two), and the fault is reported for repair.
why: Periphery reliability (fact 7): decoder faults become repairable events instead of yield or field killers.

title: One base-implant mask revives BiCMOS bipolar sense amps
idea: 1990s BiCMOS DRAMs used bipolar sense amps because Vbe matches to ~1 mV, against ~15 mV of MOS Vt mismatch. Add one p-base implant mask to the periphery flow to form vertical NPNs (the existing n-well as collector, existing n+ as emitter) and place a bipolar differential pre-amp in front of each latch group.
why: ~5-10x lower offset lets the amp resolve ~20 mV instead of ~100 mV, so Cs can shrink ~3x (fact 1) or bitlines can double in length, halving sense stripes (fact 7).

title: Liquid-nitrogen DRAM pods with four-times-longer bitlines
idea: Inverting 'DRAM runs at room temperature': operate memory racks at 77 K, where sense-amp transistors gain ~2-3x drive with less mismatch and access-transistor leakage nearly vanishes, then redesign mats with 4x longer bitlines (fewer sense amps) and refresh effectively off.
why: Sense-amp count -50-75%, refresh energy ~0 and ~15-25% density gain from freed area; cooling overhead amortized in hyperscale pods.

title: Decay-twin reference cells make sense thresholds age with data
idea: Time-shift the sense reference: each 64-cell segment carries a '1' twin and a '0' twin written at the same moment as the data, and the SA compares data cells against the twins' decayed midpoint, so the threshold follows real leakage and temperature and rows stay readable after ~80% charge loss. The refresh engine is deleted; the mats serve paused-session KV cache and stashed tensors idle 1-60 s.
why: Readable window grows ~100-1000x beyond 64 ms for median cells (tail cells mapped to spares), removing refresh's ~46 fJ/bit, 16-33% of idle power and 10-20% of bandwidth (fact 3).

title: CCD bitline marches charge packets to one edge charge amplifier
idea: Move the charge to the sensor instead of the sensor to the charge: the bitline becomes a buried CCD channel with 3-phase clock gates, cells dump their charge into it, and packets are shifted (image-sensor style) to one low-noise floating-diffusion charge amplifier at the array edge, then shifted back for restore.
why: Facts 7 and 1: one amplifier per ~512 cells instead of per bitline; CCD charge amps resolve tens of electrons, so Cs could drop from ~5 fF to <1 fF with no 60:1 pillars. Shift speed is the main risk.

title: Synaptic-scaling refresh loop holding corrected errors at a set point
idea: Neurons scale synapses to keep firing near a homeostatic set point. A controller loop stretches each rank's refresh interval additively until host/on-die ECC corrected-error counts reach a tiny target (e.g., 1 per 10^14 bit-hours). It shrinks the interval multiplicatively on any rise and snaps to the JEDEC rate when errors cluster. Firmware plus a 12-month soak on 200 DIMMs, ~$700k.
why: Fact 3: cool datacenter DIMMs could safely run 2-3x longer intervals, cutting refresh energy/bandwidth ~50% with zero hardware change.

title: Hourglass flip: precharge-free sensing starts from last value
idea: An hourglass is never reset, just flipped. Skip bitline equalization: each bitline starts from whichever rail its last sensed value left it at, a 1-bit tag per bitline group tells the SA to use a high-side or low-side reference, and a cell matching the rail moves no charge, so bitlines toggle only when data changes.
why: Precharge and equalize charge per activation becomes proportional to data change rate; for correlated or zero-heavy data (50-90% unchanged) bitline energy falls ~3-10x.

title: Canal-lock charge transfer between local and global bitlines
idea: A farmer moves water uphill with locks, not pumps. A short 64-cell local bitline gets a high charge-share ratio, then a clocked PMOS charge-transfer gate (the 'lock') moves that packet onto a pre-biased global bitline in two staged transfers, multiplying voltage by the capacitance ratio before one shared SA latches.
why: Raises effective signal 3-5x without a bigger capacitor, letting one SA serve 8 local segments and easing the ~5 fF Cs requirement (facts 1, 7).

title: Liquid-nitrogen memory: cool the DRAM, shrink the sense amps
idea: Reverse the thermal assumption: memory sleds run at 77 K in liquid nitrogen produced on site by U.S. air-separation plants (no helium); junction and GIDL leakage collapse, mobility roughly doubles and Vt mismatch tightens, allowing half-size SAs and VARY ~0.6 V.
why: Facts 3, 10 and 7: refresh power ~0, CV^2 energy ~-60%, SA area ~-40%; avoids the helium chokepoint entirely.

title: Continuous-casting sensing: no precharge, sense against the previous state
idea: Like continuous casting that never stops to pour a new ingot, bitlines are never equalized to VDD/2: they keep the last row's resolved values. The SA chooses between two references (VDD-delta or delta) based on the bitline's held previous bit, so the next activate starts at once.
why: Removes tRP (~14 ns) and equalize/precharge energy (~20-30% of activate energy), raising effective random-access bandwidth ~15-25%.

title: Display gate-on-array IGZO wordline drivers stacked above the array
idea: LCD makers moved gate drivers onto the glass as thin-film shift registers (gate-on-array). Do the same: build sub-wordline drivers and local row-decode NAND as IGZO TFT circuits in the BEOL directly over the cell array, leaving only global predecode in silicon.
why: Periphery area: sub-wordline driver stripes (~10-12% of die) go to near zero, for ~10% more bits per wafer, if IGZO TFTs tolerate the 3 V wordline swing.

title: Muralist's overpaint: oxide-TFT wordline drivers on top of the array
idea: An artist paints a second layer over the finished canvas. Build sub-wordline drivers and bitline-isolation switches as BEOL oxide-semiconductor (IGZO or IWO) TFTs above the cell array, which tolerate 3-4 V wordline levels with near-zero off-leakage, and delete the silicon SWD strips.
why: Removes ~10% of die area in high-voltage silicon periphery plus its leakage; oxide TFT breakdown suits the 3 V wordline (facts 7, 10).

title: Cross-fab sequential build: U.S. logic fab first, memory fab last
idea: Reverse the wafer-flow order: a U.S. logic fab builds periphery FEOL and a Mo-based interconnect, then ships wafers to a U.S. memory fab that grows the array above at <=450 C with laser-recrystallized Si access devices and MIM capacitors, giving monolithic CMOS-under-array across two U.S. companies without bonding.
why: Facts 7 and 4: die area ~-35% with logic-grade periphery, no HKMG module in the memory fab and no bond-yield loss.

title: Jacquard loom: coincident half-select tier addressing, no 3D staircase
idea: A Jacquard loom lifts any thread pattern by crossing hooks and cords. In 3D DRAM, replace the per-tier staircase contacts with a tier-select plate per level and a gate line per vertical pillar, each driven to about half the turn-on voltage, so only the tier-by-pillar intersection conducts, as in coincident-current core memory.
why: 3D DRAM blockers (fact 2): staircase area and per-tier drivers grow linearly with tiers; coincident selection needs N+M drivers for NxM cells and drops the staircase etch loop (~5-10 litho/etch steps at 32+ tiers).

title: Steep-slope tunnel-FET sense amps for a 0.4 V array
idea: Box: low-voltage cap x Si access x TFET cross-coupled latch x CMOS co-integration x SOI x Ge/III-V source epitaxy. TFETs with 30-40 mV/decade subthreshold slope form a latch that resolves ~15 mV signals at 0.4 V supply, letting the array voltage drop from ~1 V to 0.4 V.
why: Voltage floor: bitline CV^2 energy ~-6x and sensing power down.

title: Diode-matrix predecoders printed in BEOL above the array
idea: 1950s computers decoded addresses with passive diode matrices. Deposit a thin-film oxide Schottky diode stack (e.g., Pt/IGZO) between upper metals and wire it as a diode-AND predecode matrix directly over the cell array, so the silicon below holds only the final wordline drivers.
why: Moves ~30-40% of decoder logic off silicon, shrinking the periphery share (fact 7) by several points without EUV (fact 4).

title: Oscillation: bitline voltage tunes ring oscillators, counters compare frequency
idea: TRIZ #18 Mechanical vibration: after charge sharing, each sense node starves the supply of a tiny ring oscillator; a counter shared by 16 bitlines tallies cycles over 2-5 ns against a reference oscillator, turning a sub-10 mV difference into a digital count with built-in noise averaging, followed by a digital write-back.
why: Facts 1 and 7: frequency-domain sensing tolerates ~3-5x smaller signals and is synthesizable logic with no matched analog pairs, so it shrinks with logic nodes.

title: Honeycomb mat tiling sharing each sense-amp hub among three mats
idea: Bees' hexagonal comb shares every wall between neighbors. Mats are tiled hexagonally so each sense-amp hub sits where three mats meet and is time-multiplexed among their bitlines: one active, one as open-bitline reference, one idle. Conventional open bitline shares between only two.
why: Fact 7: sense amps per bit fall ~1/3, so the sense-amp stripe shrinks ~30% and the die ~5-7%. The cell array is already hex-packed, so lithography fits.

title: Lock-in chopper sense amp doubles cells per bitline
idea: As in a lock-in amplifier, cross-switches chop bitline vs reference at ~4 GHz during signal development; the preamp works in the modulated band and a demodulator feeds the latch, so SA offset and 1/f noise fall outside the signal band. Resolvable signal drops from ~80 mV to ~25 mV.
why: Periphery area: 1024 instead of 512 cells per bitline halves the SA stripes (~10% of die); or the same margin with ~3x smaller Cs.

title: Spiking-neuron voltage-to-delay time-domain sensing
idea: Like an integrate-and-fire neuron, the developed bitline voltage sets the discharge current of a small node, turning a 30 mV difference into a ~20 ps race; a tiny SR-latch arbiter decides whether bitline or reference fires first, with digital delay trims absorbing mismatch.
why: Periphery area: a digital-style comparator scales with logic nodes and is ~2x smaller than large matched analog SA transistors.

title: NbO2 Mott-switch sense latch replaces cross-coupled sense amplifier
idea: Effect: Mott insulator-to-metal transition. Bias a ~20 nm NbO2 threshold switch just below its transition voltage between the bitline and a reference; the cell's ~60 mV charge-sharing signal tips it across threshold, its resistance collapses ~100x in <1 ns, and one restore FET writes the row back. One BEOL device plus 1-2 FETs replaces the 6-10 transistor latch and equalizer.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp stripes are ~15-20% of die; a 3-4x smaller SA, which could also sit in BEOL above the array, frees ~10% of die area.

title: F: fluoropolymer ferroelectric caps hold trimmed reference per mat
idea: Use P(VDF-TrFE) (C, H, F) ferroelectric capacitors as partially polarized analog memories that set each mat's open-bitline reference level; at test the reference is trimmed to that mat's measured signal midpoint and held without DACs or fuses.
why: Mat-to-mat Cs and leakage variation erodes sense margin; centered references recover ~20-30 mV, buying longer refresh or smaller Cs (facts 1, 3).

title: Parametron phase-locked sense amps immune to transistor offset
idea: Revive Goto's 1954 parametron. Each sense node is a tiny resonator (MOS varactor plus active inductor) pumped at 2f, which can only oscillate in one of two phases, and the bitline's charge-sharing signal seeds which phase wins. The decision depends on the seed's sign relative to a common pump rather than on matched transistor pairs, and phase outputs can be majority-voted (parametron logic) for free in-periphery error voting.
why: Large matched sense pairs are no longer needed, so the sense stripe could shrink ~2-3x (fact 7) and work with smaller signals (fact 1).

title: Sputtered NbO2 Mott threshold switch as sense comparator
idea: Substitute the transistor comparator with a two-terminal NbO2 insulator-metal-transition device biased just below its threshold: bitline signal above the reference triggers abrupt (~ns) conduction that sets the restore driver. Reactive sputtering and e-beam pillars suffice.
why: Periphery area: a two-terminal device fits at bitline pitch in a via, shrinking sense strips ~2-3x.

title: Hair-cell stochastic resonance: dithered mini-latch with majority vote
idea: Cochlear hair cells use stochastic resonance, where added noise helps a threshold detector see sub-threshold input. An isolated mini-comparator hanging off the bitline pair gets a controlled zero-mean dither on its tail node and fires 3-5 times in ~4 ns. A majority vote sets the main latch, which then restores the cell.
why: Fact 1/7: tolerates ~40% smaller bitline swing (60 mV vs 100 mV), so bitlines can carry 1024 cells instead of 512. That halves the sense-amp count and its stripe area, roughly 5-8% of the die, or allows smaller Cs.

title: Cochlear hair cell: Hopf-bifurcation oscillator as sense amplifier
idea: Outer hair cells reach huge gain for faint sounds by sitting just below an oscillation onset (a Hopf bifurcation). Bias a 3-4 transistor local oscillator per bitline pair right at onset; the small charge-sharing signal pushes it into oscillation at phase 0 or phase pi, and a phase detector latches the bit before a restore driver writes back.
why: Capacitor charge wall: near-bifurcation compressive gain could resolve ~10-15 mV instead of ~60-100 mV, so Cs could drop ~3-5x or bitlines double in length, removing half the SA strips (~10% of die).

title: Tezzaron's split periphery fixed with in-array 16:1 preamp multiplexing
idea: Failure mined: Tezzaron's DiRAM moved sense amps onto a separate logic die but was capped by TSV pitch and lack of capital. Fix: give each bitline a 2-transistor gain preamp in the array wafer and time-multiplex 16 preamps onto one 1 um hybrid bond. Latching, write-back and ECC run on a bonded logic wafer from a mature U.S. node.
why: The array wafer becomes ~85-90% cells vs ~51% today (fact 7), ~1.7x bits per array wafer. The periphery wafer uses cheap non-EUV logic, which lowers blended capital intensity.

title: Magnetoelectric laminates harvest broadcast field to generate wordline boost voltage
idea: Effect: magnetostriction coupled to piezoelectricity. A package-level planar coil broadcasts a ~10 MHz AC magnetic field; each bank carries a FeGa (magnetostrictive) / AlScN (piezoelectric) laminate whose strain produces several volts locally, which a rectifier stores as VPP. This replaces the area-hungry switched-capacitor charge pumps and long VPP buses.
why: Periphery area/energy (facts 7, 10): VPP pumps take ~3-5% of die at ~30% efficiency; local magnetoelectric generation removes pump area and roughly halves VPP distribution loss.

title: Anodized-aluminum pore forests become dense charge-pump capacitors
idea: Borrow the architectural-aluminum anodizing line: anodize a sputtered Al layer over the periphery so it self-assembles hexagonal pores ~150 nm wide and 2-3 um deep. Line the pores with a CVD TiN/Ta2O5/TiN stack (a 1990s DRAM capacitor stack) to make 3D capacitors stacked above the pump and decoupling circuits.
why: ~100-200 fF/um^2 vs ~10-20 fF/um^2 for MOS caps: VPP/VBB pump and decap area (several % of die) shrinks ~5-10x using only a wet bench and CVD.

title: Wavelength-addressed wordline decoding with silicon microring filters
idea: Broadcast the row address as a WDM optical comb on a waveguide running over each bank; each sub-wordline driver group has a microring tuned to one wavelength plus a photodiode that fires its driver. The predecoder tree and its long, repeated global wires disappear, because a photonic add-drop filter now does the row decoder's job.
why: Periphery (fact 7) and data movement (fact 5): removes global decode wiring; ~30% lower decode energy and area in large banks, with optical I/O as a natural extension.

title: Cu: hybrid-bond periphery wafers from idle U.S. mature-node fabs
idea: Split each DRAM into an array-only wafer from the DRAM fab and a periphery wafer (decoders, I/O, control, SA back-ends) made on 28-65 nm logic lines in U.S. fabs, joined by Cu-Cu hybrid bonding at ~1 um pitch.
why: Frees ~40% of expensive DRAM-fab wafer area per die for cells (facts 4, 7) and puts underused U.S. capacity to work (U.S. manufacturability); periphery gets faster logic transistors.

title: Roving sense amp visits sampled bitlines in picosecond turns
idea: Time jump inside one row cycle: each bitline gets a tiny isolation switch that freezes its charge-shared signal, then one fast SA on a ~100 ps cycle visits 8 bitlines in turn, resolving and writing back each, like the column-shared ADCs of image sensors. SA count falls 8x for ~4 ns of added serial latency per segment.
why: SA stripes are a large slice of the ~49% periphery (fact 7); 8x fewer SAs cuts SA-stripe area ~60-70% net of switches, roughly 8-12% of die area.

title: Only one sense amp per 16 bitlines: bitline charge queue
idea: Self-imposed limit: one sense amp per 16 bitlines. After the wordline fires, each bitline holds its charge-shared signal on its own ~40 fF capacitance behind an isolation switch, and one offset-compensated sense amp resolves and writes back the 16 bitlines one after another in ~2 ns slots while the wordline stays open; the requested slice is resolved first and the rest are restored in the background.
why: Periphery (fact 7): the sense-amp stripe is ~15-20% of the die, and sharing cuts its area ~8-10x (die area -10-12%). The cost is a longer tRAS for full-row restore, which hides behind fine-grained access.

title: Negative-capacitance ferroelectric gate gives sense pair internal gain
idea: Add a thin HZO negative-capacitance layer in the gate stack of the sense amplifier's input pair so the internal channel potential swings more than the bitline (body factor < 1), amplifying a 50 mV signal ~2x before the latch fires.
why: Halves required cell signal or doubles tolerated Cbl (fact 1); longer bitlines cut SA count (fact 7).

title: Log-domain time-to-threshold sensing keeps decayed gain cells readable
idea: Time-domain sensing: gain cells are read by timing how long the read current takes to discharge a sense node, decided on a log-time scale; since subthreshold read current is exponential in stored voltage, a '1' that has lost 0.6 V still discharges ~10^3x faster than a '0', so cells stay readable 3-10x longer, reaching minutes, and session KV caches need no refresh.
why: Stretches gain-cell retention past session idle times, deleting refresh (fact 3); the log scale also absorbs temperature drift.

title: Resonant LC tank drives wordlines adiabatically, recycling boost energy
idea: Fuse resonant-clock-mesh design with wordline drive: wordlines in a bank charge from a sinusoidal resonant VPP rail set by an on-package inductor, so energy swings between the inductor and the wordline capacitance instead of being dumped to ground at every precharge.
why: Voltage floor (fact 10): recovers ~60-70% of ~3 V wordline CV^2 energy, ~20-25% lower activation energy.

title: Tin-can telephone: 60 mV ground-referenced global data lines
idea: A tin-can telephone carries a voice on a whisper of energy. Drive the mm-long on-die global data lines with ground-referenced ~60 mV swings from capacitively divided drivers and receive with clocked offset-trimmed sense amps, instead of full 1.1 V CMOS swings.
why: Global data-line energy scales with swing x supply: 60 mV vs ~1 V cuts it ~10-15x; global I/O is ~20-30% of DRAM access energy.

title: Art restorer's field retouching: relaxed screening plus in-field PPR
idea: A restorer fixes cracks as they appear instead of discarding the painting. Ship dies screened at a looser sense-margin limit, and let the host's existing patrol scrub find weak rows and remap them with DDR5's existing soft and hard post-package repair commands.
why: Lowers test yield loss and burn-in time (+3-6% supply, lower test cost) using only JEDEC commands.

title: Frequency-addressed MEMS resonators select mats over one wire
idea: Give each mat's enable a MEMS resonator relay with a unique resonant frequency on a shared bus; driving the bus at f_k rings up only resonator k and closes its mat switch, replacing a mat-select decoder tree with one address wire (orthogonal frequency channels as the address code).
why: Removes global decoder wiring and pre-decode buffers from the periphery (fact 7); suits slow mat power-up/select, not ns row access.

title: Socketed HBM base die rescues good DRAM dies from failed stacks
idea: Ideal result: a stack that is never scrapped. Join the periphery/base logic die to the DRAM stack with low-temperature indium micro-bumps and a removable clamp frame instead of underfill, so a failed base die or bad bottom joint is swapped at ~160 C and the good DRAM dies are reused.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): recovers much of the 20-30% stack yield loss; the base die becomes a field-replaceable part.

title: Hopf-critical oscillator sense amp poised at edge of oscillation
idea: Cochlear outer hair cells sit near a Hopf bifurcation for huge gain on faint sound. A tiny oscillator is biased just below onset, so a few-mV bitline differential tips it into oscillation whose starting phase encodes the bit, captured by a flip-flop in ~2 ns. Proven on an open 130 nm shuttle with on-chip bitline/cell-cap replicas for <$1M in 24 months.
why: Fact 1/7: gain near criticality (>40 dB at microamp bias) could halve the required bitline signal, enabling longer bitlines with fewer sense amps or smaller Cs.

title: Open-bitline 4F^2 vertical cells, coupling noise absorbed by code
idea: Box: vertical-channel 4F^2 cell x VCT access x open-bitline SA without dummy mats x tight-pitch array x bulk Si x standard. Accept the higher bitline-to-bitline coupling noise and weaker reference symmetry of open-bitline 4F^2 arrays, and delete edge dummy mats, letting ~1% of reads fail and be corrected.
why: Density: 6F^2 to 4F^2 (+50% bits per area) and no dummy-mat overhead (~3-5%).

title: Room-temperature nanocluster single-electron electrometer as sense element
idea: Molecule-scale jump: a sub-2 nm metal-nanocluster single-electron transistor (charging energy >10 kT) at each short bitline segment counts tens of electrons, so a cell needs only ~0.02-0.05 fF (the storage gate itself) and no capacitor.
why: Deletes the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and opens 4F2 and 3D cells (fact 2); 3-5x density if SET variability is tamed.

title: Back-gate trimmed tiny sense amps replace large matched pairs
idea: Worse: make sense-amp transistors huge so random mismatch stays below the signal. Flip: shrink sense-amp devices 3-4x and cancel each pair's offset with a per-column back-gate voltage programmed at wafer test from a shared trim DAC row and held as a fuse code.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): sense-amp strips ~40-50% smaller while tolerating smaller cell signals.

title: Bat-echolocation TDR to find and remap marginal HBM TSVs
idea: Bats map their world from echo delays. Picosecond time-domain reflectometry through HBM test and boundary-scan paths measures impedance discontinuities in each TSV/microbump lane, flags marginal (resistive or voided) ones before they fail, and remaps them to HBM's existing spare lanes. Instrument plus algorithm work on stack samples, ~$800k in 24 months.
why: Fact 6: TSV/bump defects drive much of the 20-30% stack yield loss. Earlier, finer detection with remap could recover several points of yield and cut HBM cost/bit.

title: 2050 faith in codes: double-length bitlines guarded by on-die ECC
idea: A 2050 engineer accepts noisy sensing and corrects it. Double bitline length to 1024-2048 cells per sense amp, accept a raw sense error rate near 1e-6, and absorb it with DDR5's mandatory on-die ECC widened internally to longer codewords; the host still sees standard DDR5.
why: Halves bitline sense-amp stripes (~8-10% die area, fact 7) with an interface-transparent fix.

title: Eliminate full-row activation with dual-gate cells selected by row AND column
idea: Give each access transistor a second gate tied to a column-segment select line, so a channel conducts only when both its wordline and its 64-bit column segment are high. Only the addressed bits share charge, sense and restore, instead of all 8,192 cells on the row.
why: Fact 8: cuts the 128x overfetch and ~5.9 pJ per useful bit to ~0.3-0.6 pJ, and SA activity drops ~95% on random reads; cell area grows ~30-50%.

title: Segmented sub-wordline gates activate only the requested 512-byte slice
idea: Worse: open an entire 8 KB row to read 64 bytes. Flip: insert segment-select transistors in the sub-wordline drivers so only the cells and sense amps of one 512 B slice connect and fire, leaving the rest of the row untouched.
why: Destructive read and 128x overfetch (fact 8): activation energy per useful bit drops ~10-16x and row-hammer exposure per activation shrinks.

title: Automata Processor salvaged as a sense-amp key-match GET engine
idea: Failure mined: Micron's Automata Processor put state machines next to DRAM arrays and died on an alien programming model. Fix: add one XOR plus wired-NOR comparator per 64 sense amps and expose a single command, GET(key). A broadcast key is matched against every key in the open row (one hash bucket), and only the matching value leaves the chip.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and overfetch (fact 8): hash and key-value lookups move 64 B instead of 8 KB, ~100x fewer bits on the bus, for ~1-2% of SA-stripe area.

title: Fractional-distillation sensing: one timed comparator reads multi-level cells
idea: Like a distillation column where each fraction boils off at its own temperature, each 2T gain cell's stored level sets how fast its read bitline discharges, and a single comparator timestamps the threshold crossing. Early/mid/late/no crossing yields 2 bits per cell from one comparator and a shared counter instead of three SAs per bitline.
why: Enables 2-bit/cell DRAM-class arrays (2x density) without tripling SA area; sensing periphery per bit roughly halves.

title: Array-only DRAM wafer with periphery bonded from US 28nm logic
idea: Inverting 'cells and periphery share one wafer process': the DRAM fab builds wafers with only access devices, bitlines and capacitors (no periphery transistors, fewer implants and masks), while sense amps, decoders and I/O are made on a 28nm logic wafer in a US foundry and hybrid-bonded face-to-face at ~1 um pitch along every subarray edge.
why: Periphery (~49% of die) leaves the expensive EUV DRAM wafer, so bits per DRAM wafer rise ~1.7-1.9x, periphery moves onto depreciated US logic capacity, and sense amps get faster logic transistors.

title: Eliminate scanners for periphery: imprint with hydrocarbon-release molds
idea: Pattern the 40-100 nm periphery layers by jet-and-flash nanoimprint using an acrylate resist with no fluorinated surfactant and a mold anti-stick layer of octadecylsilane instead of the usual fluorosilane. Transfer the pattern with Cl2/HBr/O2 etches only.
why: Removes optical scanners, PFAS photoacid generators and fluorinated topcoats from ~10-15 periphery layers; litho capex on those layers ~-70% (fact 4).

title: Bunk bed: oxide thin-film decoders stacked above the cell array
idea: Put the decoders upstairs like a bunk bed: build row predecoders, wordline-driver pull-ups and column-select logic from BEOL W-doped In2O3 or IGZO thin-film transistors (as in LCD gate-on-array drivers) directly over the array at <=400 C, connected down by vias, leaving only sense amps in silicon.
why: Periphery area (fact 7): decoders and drivers are ~15-20% of die; stacking them gives ~15% more bits per wafer with no EUV, and oxide TFTs tolerate the 3 V wordline swing.

title: Hydroforming wordlines: bootstrapped local boost replaces high-voltage drivers
idea: Like hydroforming, which shapes metal with uniform fluid pressure instead of heavy punches, precharge each local wordline to VDD through a small thin-oxide device, float it, then pressurize it to ~3 V by capacitive coupling from a shared boost line. This revives the 1970s NMOS bootstrap, so no thick-oxide PMOS is needed at every wordline.
why: Sub-wordline driver strips (~8-10% of die) shrink ~40% because the thick-oxide PMOS and well spacing go away; works with 180 nm devices.
